Digital artist nohygiene creates surreal 3D characters that combine angelic imagery, early-internet aesthetics and intensely emotional scenes. Her recurring figures have oversized heads, metallic or pale bodies, long hair and wings. They appear alone, exhausted, in love or overwhelmed, while simple symbols such (Artvangarde)as hearts, fire and tears make their emotions immediately visible. The deliberately imperfect graphics recall early 3D animation, online avatars and old computer imagery, rather than the polished realism of contemporary CGI. It emerged as a subculture in the early 2010s through internet fashion communities, especially on platforms like Tumblr. Unlike classic goth fashion, which is usually dominated by black clothing, dark makeup, and a more serious atmosphere, pastel goth mixes dark themes with cute or dreamy visuals. Common colors include pastel pink, lavender, mint, baby blue, and white, often paired with black accents. The style frequently includes oversized sweaters, skirts, platform shoes, chokers, harnesses, fishnets, crosses, chains, bows, and accessories inspired by alternative Japanese fashion. Hairstyles often feature dyed hair in pastel shades such as pink, lilac, or silver. Visually, pastel goth combines motifs like skulls, bats, moons, crosses, and occult symbols with soft elements such as hearts, plush toys, clouds, and candy-like color palettes. This contrast creates an aesthetic that feels both cute and dark at the same time. Pastel goth also strongly influenced digital art, photography, and online aesthetics. In artwork, it is often represented through soft lighting, dreamy pastel tones, melancholic characters, gothic fashion details, and surreal or dark fantasy themes.

What do people actually mean when they talk about “digital” TV? In this clip, I asked @Claire @ Glasgow Tellyfest “digital” really means when we talk about making television in a new way.  Her point was simple: it’s not about shooting something on your phone. It’s about how audiences consume stories. People don’t always sit down for an hour anymore. They watch in shorter bursts. They follow creators over years. They expect intimacy, direct address, and a different relationship between storyteller and audience. Digital isn’t just a lower-budget version of television. Want to create and sell digital products? Here's what you actually do. 👇  1. Start with a problem. What problem are you solving for someone else? The best digital products make something easier, faster, or less overwhelming. 2. Create the solution. Turn what you know into something useful—a guide, checklist, planner, workbook, template, printable, mini-course, or resource. 3. Choose where to sell it. You can sell digital products through platforms like Etsy, Teachers Pay Teachers, Stan Store, or your own website. Choose the platform that makes sense for your product and audience. You can also publish them on Amazon Kindle Direct Publishing or Google Play.  4. Market it. Creating the product is only HALF the job. People have to find it! Use Pinterest, TikTok,  email, a blog, or search-friendly content to show people how your product solves their problem. 5. Learn from the first one...then create another. Your first product doesn't have to build financial freedom. It's your starting point. Create one useful product. Learn how to sell it. Improve. Then create another. Over time, you can build a collection of digital products that can be purchased while you're teaching, spending time with family, or simply living your life.  That's what I love about learning skills that can create income from home. I'm not looking for another job. I'm building more ways to earn—and more choices for my future. Financial freedom doesn't have to start with something huge. It can start with one product that solves one problem.
